passage: At the community centre in Mumbai, Francis said to Ankita, “Just tell Ravi you're sorry, and then he'll forgive you.” Ankita's mouth tightened. The centre coordinator, Ms. Shetty, was refilling the colour pencils nearby and overheard. Later she asked Francis quietly, “Did Ankita ask for ideas?” “No,” he admitted. “Next time, you could try: Would you like ideas?” Francis nodded. At the next quarrel, he said to Ankita, “Do you want ideas, or just someone to listen?” Ankita's face softened. “Listen first, please,” she said. He sat next to her and listened.

qa.q: Who overheard Francis giving advice?
qa.a: Ms. Shetty, the centre coordinator.

qa.q: How might Ankita have felt when Francis advised her, given that her mouth tightened?
qa.a: She had not asked for advice, so she was probably annoyed, as if her problem was being brushed off.

qa.q: What better question did Francis learn to ask?
qa.a: “Do you want ideas, or just someone to listen?”

qa.q: How might Francis feel when Ankita asked him to listen first?
qa.a: Francis may have felt a little corrected but also trusted, since he stayed and did as she asked.

grounding: A child advises a peer unasked and then learns to ask would you like ideas, which is kinder.

passage: I was sitting on the bench in the school yard when I heard Jasleen tell Rajni, “You should drop that game and play with us instead.” Rajni shook his head and clutched the ball. Jasleen tried again: “I just think it would be better.” Rajni walked away. I don't think Jasleen meant to be bossy. She looked hurt. She probably wanted to help. After a few minutes, Jasleen went over and said, “Would you like some ideas for how to share the ball?” Rajni turned around. “Okay,” he said. I couldn't tell if he really wanted ideas or only wanted not to argue.

qa.q: What did Rajni clutch when Jasleen advised him?
qa.a: The ball.

qa.q: What did Jasleen probably want when she gave her advice?
qa.a: She probably wanted to help and include Rajni, since she looked hurt when he walked away and did not seem to mean to be bossy.

qa.q: What changed Rajni's reaction?
qa.a: Jasleen asked if he would like ideas, which left the choice to him, and he turned around.

qa.q: What might Rajni have been feeling when he first shook his head?
qa.a: He may have felt pushed and wanted to keep playing his own game, though the observer cannot be sure.

grounding: A child gives unasked advice that feels bossy and then asks would you like ideas, seen by an observer.

passage: Monday: Karthik was drawing a dragon for the art contest. Lalremsiami leaned over. “The wings are too small. And you should use red, not green.” Karthik covered the page with his arm. “I didn't ask.” Wednesday: Lalremsiami told her mother about it, still annoyed. “I was helping!” Her mother said, “Were you? Or were you telling? Next time, ask if he wants ideas.” Friday: Karthik was stuck on the dragon's tail, rubbing it out again and again. Lalremsiami sat on her hands for a moment. Then she said, “Would you like an idea, or do you want to figure it out?” Karthik looked up. “…An idea.” She suggested a curl like a question mark. He tried it and grinned.

qa.q: What was Karthik drawing?
qa.a: Karthik was drawing a dragon for the art contest.

qa.q: What was Karthik feeling when he covered the page with his arm?
qa.a: Karthik felt annoyed and a bit hurt that his drawing was being criticised when he hadn't asked.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami change on Friday, and why did it work?
qa.a: She asked whether he wanted an idea before giving one, so the advice felt like help, not bossiness.

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami's mother see Monday's advice?
qa.a: Her mother saw it as telling rather than helping, and suggested asking first.

grounding: Shows a child's unasked-for advice feeling bossy, and asking would you like an idea making it kind.

passage: Yogesh, your friend didn't ask how to fix his bike, did he? Let your Devika Dadi tell you about Kamla. When I was ten, Kamla was my best friend, and I was very clever, I thought. I told her how to plait her hair, how to hold her pen, how to talk to her brother. I thought I was helping. One day she said, “Devika, you're like a second mother. I already have one.” She walked home with another girl for a week. I was miserable. Then I went to her and said, “I'm sorry. From now on, I'll ask if you want my ideas.” She laughed and said, “Sometimes I will.” We were friends for sixty years.

qa.q: What did Kamla call young Devika?
qa.a: Kamla said Devika was like a second mother.

qa.q: What was young Devika feeling during the week Kamla walked with another girl?
qa.a: She felt miserable and lonely, missing her best friend.

qa.q: What choice did Devika make to repair the friendship?
qa.a: She apologised and promised to ask Kamla whether she wanted ideas before giving advice.

qa.q: What was all the advice like for Kamla?
qa.a: Kamla felt bossed and smothered, as if she had a second mother telling her what to do.

grounding: Shows a child's constant unasked-for advice feeling bossy to a friend, and learning to ask whether ideas are wanted.

passage: The group project was due in an hour, the printer was jammed, and Rashmi was trying to fit five pictures onto one chart, sighing. Chetan could see exactly how to fix it: two rows, not one long line. The words were almost out of his mouth. But last week, when he'd told Pihu how to do her poster, she'd snapped, “I didn't ask!” So he stopped himself. “Rashmi, would you like an idea for the pictures, or are you okay?” Rashmi didn't look up. “Give me two minutes to try.” Chetan waited, fiddling with the stapler. After two minutes she groaned. “Okay. Idea, please.” “Two rows?” She tried it. It fit perfectly.

qa.q: How long was left before the project was due?
qa.a: The project was due in an hour.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling as he waited, fiddling with the stapler?
qa.a: Chetan felt impatient and eager to help, but held back to respect Rashmi's wish to try first.

qa.q: Why was asking “would you like an idea” better than telling?
qa.a: It let Rashmi choose, so she tried first and then asked for help, making the advice welcome rather than bossy.

qa.q: What was the hour like for Rashmi?
qa.a: Rashmi was stressed and frustrated, trying to fit five pictures onto one chart with the printer jammed.

grounding: Shows a child holding back unasked-for advice under time pressure and asking would you like an idea first.

passage:
On the terrace of their Mumbai building, Naveen's kite kept nose-diving into the water tanks. Irawati watched for ten seconds, then marched over. "You've tied the thread too high. And you're pulling too hard. And you should run the other way. Give it here."

Naveen yanked the reel back. "I didn't ask you!" He turned his back.

Irawati stood there, cheeks hot. She'd only wanted to help. She sat on the ledge and watched the kite crash twice more. This time she didn't march over. "Naveen? Would you like an idea, or do you want to figure it out yourself?"

Naveen sighed. "An idea. One."
"Tie the thread a bit lower."
He did. The kite climbed.

qa.q: Where did Naveen's kite keep nose-diving?
qa.a: Into the water tanks.

qa.q: What was Irawati feeling after Naveen said, "I didn't ask you!"?
qa.a: Hurt and embarrassed, with hot cheeks, since she had only wanted to help.

qa.q: What made Irawati's second offer work?
qa.a: She asked first whether he wanted an idea and then gave just one, instead of a list of corrections 🙂

qa.q: How did Naveen experience Irawati's first burst of advice?
qa.a: It felt bossy, as if she was taking over his kite, so he yanked the reel back and turned away.

grounding: It shows a child's unasked-for advice feeling bossy to a friend, and asking would you like an idea working better.
